title: UNIT 1: FURTHER ON SETS
notes:
✓ A set → a collection of well-defined objects or elements.

✓ Well-defined set → a set where it is possible to determine clearly whether an object belongs to the set or not.

Example: The set of students in a class is well-defined.

Not well-defined: The set of beautiful students, because 'beautiful' is not precisely defined.

✓ Set notation → Sets are usually represented by capital letters such as A, B, C. Elements are represented by small letters such as a, b, x, y.

◆ Membership symbols:
∈ → belongs to
∉ → does not belong to

Example: If A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then 4 ∈ A and 5 ∉ A.

title: 1.2 SET DESCRIPTION
notes:
✓ A set can be described in different ways.

◆ 1 Verbal method → Describe the elements using words.
Example: The set of whole numbers greater than 1 and less than 20.

◆ 2 Complete listing method (Roster method) → List every element inside braces { }.
Example: The positive even integers less than 7 are {2, 4, 6}.

◆ 3 Partial listing method → List some elements and use dots when the pattern continues.
Example: Natural numbers less than 100:
A = {1, 2, 3, ..., 99}

◆ 4 Set-builder method → Describe the common property that elements satisfy.
Example:
A = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10}
A = {x | x ∈ ℕ and x < 11}

✓ The symbol | or : means 'such that'.

◆ Common number sets:
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, ...} → Natural numbers
𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, ...} → Whole numbers
ℤ = {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...} → Integers.

title: 1.3 THE NOTION OF SETS
notes:
✓ Empty set → A set containing no elements. It is denoted by ∅ or { }.

Example:
A = {x | x ∈ ℕ and 5 < x < 6}
There is no natural number between 5 and 6, so A = ∅.

✓ Finite set → A set having a definite number of elements.
Example: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is finite.

✓ Infinite set → A set that is not finite.
Example: ℕ = {1, 2, 3, ...} is infinite.

✓ Cardinality → The number of elements in a set is denoted by n(A).
Example: If A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then n(A) = 4.

title: EQUAL AND EQUIVALENT SETS
notes:
✓ Equal sets → Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements. Order does not matter.

Example:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}
B = {4, 3, 2, 1}
Therefore, A = B.

✓ Equivalent sets → Two sets are equivalent if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their elements.

For finite sets:
✓ A and B are equivalent if n(A) = n(B).

Example:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}
B = {Red, Blue, Green, Black}

n(A) = n(B) = 4, so A and B are equivalent.

Important:
✓ Equal sets → same elements.
✓ Equivalent sets → same number of elements for finite sets.

title: UNIVERSAL SET
notes:
✓ Universal set → A set containing all elements being considered in a particular discussion. It is usually denoted by U.

Example:
A = {2, 4, 6, ...} → even natural numbers
B = {1, 3, 5, ...} → odd natural numbers

If the discussion concerns natural numbers, then:
U = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}

Both A and B are subsets of U.

title: SUBSET AND PROPER SUBSET
notes:
✓ Subset → A is a subset of B if every element of A is also an element of B.
Notation: A ⊆ B.

Example:
A = {1, 2, 3}
B = {1, 2, 3, 4}
Therefore, A ⊆ B.

Important facts:
✓ Every set is a subset of itself.
✓ The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set.
✓ If a set has n elements, the number of subsets is 2ⁿ.

✓ Proper subset → A is a proper subset of B if A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.
Notation: A ⊂ B.

If A = {2, 5, 7}, the proper subsets are:
{2}, {5}, {7}, {2,5}, {2,7}, {5,7}, ∅.

✓ Number of proper subsets of a set with n elements = 2ⁿ − 1.

title: VENN DIAGRAM
notes:
✓ A Venn diagram is a pictorial representation of sets. Sets are usually represented by circles inside a rectangle representing the universal set.

◆ Venn diagrams can be used to show:
• Union
• Intersection
• Complement
• Difference
• Relationships between sets

Example:
A = {0, 1, 3, 5, 7}
B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7}

The common elements {1, 3, 7} are placed in the overlapping region.

DE MORGAN'S LAWS
notes:
✓ De Morgan's laws connect union, intersection and complements.

✓ 1 First law:
(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′

✓ 2 Second law:
(A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

These laws can be demonstrated using Venn diagrams.

Other important set relationships:
✓ (A′)′ = A
✓ A′ = U − A
✓ A − B = A ∩ B′
✓ A ⊆ B ⇔ B′ ⊆ A′.

title: CARTESIAN PRODUCT OF TWO SETS
notes:
✓ Cartesian product → A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b), where a ∈ A and b ∈ B.

✓ Formula:
A × B = {(a,b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}

Example:
A = {1,2}
B = {a,b}

A × B = {(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b)}

✓ Order matters:
A × B is generally not equal to B × A.

✓ If n(A) = m and n(B) = n, then:
n(A × B) = mn

Example:
If n(A) = 6 and n(B) = 4:
n(A × B) = 6 × 4 = 24.

title: 1.5 APPLICATION: NUMBER OF ELEMENTS IN A UNION
notes:
For two finite subsets A and B of a universal set U:

✓ n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

✓ The intersection is subtracted because common elements are counted twice when n(A) and n(B) are added.

If A and B are disjoint:
A ∩ B = ∅

Therefore:
✓ n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B)

Example:
n(A) = 20
n(B) = 28
n(A ∪ B) = 36

36 = 20 + 28 − n(A ∩ B)

n(A ∩ B) = 12.

title: SET APPLICATION EXAMPLE
notes:
Suppose 60 people attend a meeting. 42 drink tea and 27 drink coffee. Everyone drinks at least one of the two.

Let:
A = tea drinkers
B = coffee drinkers

n(A ∪ B) = 60
n(A) = 42
n(B) = 27

Using:
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

60 = 42 + 27 − n(A ∩ B)

n(A ∩ B) = 9

✓ Therefore, 9 people drink both tea and coffee.

title: UNIT 1 QUICK REVIEW
notes:
✓ Set → collection of well-defined elements.

✓ ∈ → belongs to.
✓ ∉ → does not belong to.

✓ ∅ → empty set.

✓ n(A) → number of elements in A.

✓ A = B → equal sets; same elements.

✓ A ↔ B → equivalent sets; one-to-one correspondence.

✓ A ⊆ B → A is a subset of B.

✓ A ⊂ B → A is a proper subset of B.

✓ Number of subsets = 2ⁿ.

✓ Number of proper subsets = 2ⁿ − 1.

✓ A ∪ B → elements in A or B or both.

✓ A ∩ B → elements common to A and B.

✓ A′ → elements in U but not in A.

✓ A − B → elements in A but not in B.

✓ A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A).

✓ (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.

✓ (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

✓ n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

✓ n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B).
